VAULT-001: Hokusai was around seventy when he designed this for a series of views of Mount Fuji, the small peak in the middle. It's a woodblock print, made in the thousands and cheap enough for ordinary people to buy. The deep blue is Prussian blue, a pigment newly arrived from Europe.
LIT-010: Fewer than a dozen of Dickinson's poems were printed while she was alive. After she died in 1886 her sister found hundreds of poems in her room. Nearly eighteen hundred are now known. The first collection came out in 1890, with the punctuation and some of the wording changed by the editors.
LIT-041: Mary Shelley began Frankenstein in the summer of 1816 at Lake Geneva, when Lord Byron proposed that each of the company write a ghost story. She was eighteen. The novel was published without her name in 1818. It is told through the letters of a ship's captain, Walton, who meets Frankenstein in the Arctic.
VAULT-257: A triptych, with Eden on the left, hell on the right, and in the middle a garden full of naked figures, giant birds and fruit. It was hanging in a nobleman's palace in Brussels by 1517. What Bosch meant by the centre panel has been debated for five hundred years. It is in the Prado.
VAULT-258: An army of skeletons overruns the land and kills everyone it meets, from the king in the corner to the peasants and the card players. Plague and war were regular facts of life in Bruegel's time. The painting is in the Prado in Madrid.
VAULT-261: Friedrich built this landscape in the studio from sketches he had made in the sandstone hills south of Dresden. He often painted figures from behind, so that the viewer looks with them. Who the man is, if anyone, is not known. The painting is in the Kunsthalle in Hamburg.
VAULT-262: Munch said the idea came on a walk above the Oslo fjord at sunset, when he felt a great scream pass through nature. He made four versions and a print. This one, from 1893, is in the National Museum in Oslo. A faint pencil note on it saying only a madman could have painted it was confirmed in 2021 to be in Munch's own hand.
VAULT-263: This is a tronie, a study of a character or expression, and no specific sitter is known. In 1881 it was sold at auction in The Hague for two guilders, because it was dirty and nobody recognised it. It is now the best-known painting in the Netherlands, at the Mauritshuis.
VAULT-264: The five-year-old princess Margarita with her maids, in a room of the royal palace in Madrid. Velázquez painted himself in at the easel. The king and queen appear in the mirror on the back wall. The red cross on his chest was added later, after he was made a knight in 1659.
VAULT-363: The painting that made Fuseli famous when it was shown in London in 1782. Prints of it sold across Europe. The 'mare' in 'nightmare' is an old word for a spirit that sits on the chest of a sleeper, and has nothing to do with horses, though Fuseli put one in. It is in the Detroit Institute of Arts.
VAULT-366: Painted a few months after the revolution of July 1830, which drove the last Bourbon king from France. Delacroix did not fight but wrote that if he had not fought for his country he could at least paint for her. The new government bought the picture and then kept it out of sight for years as too inflammatory.
VAULT-382: Böcklin painted five versions of this between 1880 and 1886, and this is the first. He never explained it, and the title came from his dealer. It became one of the most reproduced pictures in Germany. Rachmaninoff wrote a piece of music about it after seeing a black-and-white print.
VAULT-392: Painted in 1907–08, at the height of the period when Klimt used gold leaf, after seeing the Byzantine mosaics in Ravenna. The Austrian state bought it from an exhibition before he had finished it. It is in the Belvedere in Vienna.
VAULT-408: The second and larger of Artemisia's two paintings of Judith killing the Assyrian general. As a teenager she had been raped by a painter who worked with her father, and she gave evidence at his trial in 1612. The painting has often been linked to that history. It is in the Uffizi in Florence.
LIT-002: Moby-Dick sold badly when it came out in 1851, and reviewers were puzzled by it. Melville gave up trying to live by writing and worked for nineteen years as a customs inspector in New York. The book was out of print when he died in 1891. Its reputation dates from the 1920s.
LIT-007: Shelley wrote Ozymandias at the end of 1817 in a friendly contest with another poet, Horace Smith, who published his own sonnet on the same subject a few weeks later. Ozymandias is the Greek name for the pharaoh Ramesses II. A huge fragment of one of his statues was then on its way to the British Museum.
LIT-014: From Songs of Experience, 1794. Blake wrote it as a companion to The Lamb in his earlier Songs of Innocence. His notebook shows that he worked through several drafts.
LIT-017: Yeats wrote this in January 1919. The First World War had just ended, Russia was in revolution, and fighting was beginning in Ireland. His pregnant wife had nearly died in the influenza pandemic a few weeks earlier. The poem was published in 1920.
LIT-018: The Raven was published in a New York newspaper in January 1845 and made Poe famous almost overnight. It was reprinted everywhere and widely parodied. He was paid very little for it.
LIT-034: Wilfred Owen drafted this poem in 1917 at a military hospital in Scotland, where he was being treated for shell shock. The Latin title is from Horace and means 'it is sweet and fitting'. Owen went back to the front and was killed one week before the war ended. Most of his poems were published after his death.
LIT-040: Henley wrote this in 1875 in a hospital in Edinburgh. He had lost one leg to tuberculosis of the bone, and spent nearly two years there while the surgeon Joseph Lister worked to save the other. Nelson Mandela recited the poem to fellow prisoners on Robben Island.
LIT-042: According to Coleridge's own preface, he fell asleep after taking opium, composed two or three hundred lines in a dream, and was writing them down when a visitor on business interrupted him. When he got back to his desk the rest was gone. He kept the fragment for nearly twenty years, and published it in 1816 at Byron's urging.
LIT-054: The closing sections of the poem that opened the first edition of Leaves of Grass. Whitman published the book himself in 1855 and set some of the type with his own hands. It had twelve poems and no author's name on the title page. He went on revising and enlarging it for the rest of his life.
LIT-092: Kafka wrote The Metamorphosis in three weeks at the end of 1912 and published it in 1915. When the book was being designed, he wrote to the publisher insisting that the insect itself must not be shown on the cover, not even from a distance.
LIT-503: Frost wrote this in 1915 as a gentle joke on his friend Edward Thomas, who on their walks together could never pick a path without regretting the other one. Thomas took it seriously, as most readers have since. It opens Frost's 1916 collection Mountain Interval.
LIT-505: Published in 1922. Eliot wrote much of it while recovering from a breakdown, partly at the English seaside and partly in a clinic in Switzerland. Ezra Pound then cut the draft roughly in half, and Eliot dedicated the poem to him.
VAULT-505: Leonardo is believed to have begun this portrait in Florence around 1503 and to have taken it with him to France in 1516. The sitter is identified as Lisa del Giocondo, born into the Gherardini family, the wife of a Florentine silk merchant. The painting was stolen from the Louvre in August 1911 and returned there in January 1914.
VAULT-506: Leonardo painted this on a wall of the refectory of the convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. It shows the moment after Jesus tells the apostles that one of them will betray him. Leonardo did not use fresco but painted in tempera on a sealed wall, and by 1517 the paint was starting to flake.
VAULT-507: Van Gogh painted this in June 1889 at the asylum of Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he had admitted himself a month earlier. It shows the view from his east-facing window before sunrise, with a village added from imagination. The Museum of Modern Art in New York has owned it since 1941.
VAULT-509: The goddess Venus arrives at the shore on a shell, blown by the wind god Zephyrus, after her birth from the sea. Botticelli probably painted it in the mid-1480s. It is on canvas, a cheaper support than the wood panel of his Primavera, which is also in the Uffizi.
VAULT-510: One of nine scenes from the Book of Genesis that Michelangelo painted along the centre of the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512. Pope Julius II commissioned the ceiling.
VAULT-513: A group portrait of an Amsterdam civic guard company under Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, painted in 1642. The scene is not a night scene; the name came from the dark varnish that long covered it. The canvas was trimmed on all four sides in 1715, when it was moved to Amsterdam's town hall.
VAULT-514: French soldiers shoot citizens of Madrid in reprisal for the uprising of 2 May 1808 against Napoleon's occupation. Goya painted it in 1814, after the French had been driven out of Spain. It has a companion picture of the same size, The Second of May 1808.
VAULT-520: Grant Wood saw this small wooden house, with its Gothic-style upper window, in Eldon, Iowa. He painted the kind of people he imagined living in it, using his sister and his dentist as models. The Art Institute of Chicago bought the painting in 1930, the year it was made.
LIT-535: Frost wrote the poem in June 1922 at his farmhouse in Shaftsbury, Vermont. It was published in 1923 in New Hampshire, the collection that won him the first of his four Pulitzer Prizes.
VAULT-534: Picasso painted this in Paris in 1907 after months of preparatory sketches. It shows five women in a brothel on the Carrer d'Avinyó in Barcelona. He kept it largely out of public view until 1916, and the Museum of Modern Art acquired it in 1939.
VAULT-539: Duchamp submitted a porcelain urinal, signed R. Mutt, to the 1917 exhibition of the Society of Independent Artists in New York, and the board declined to show it. The original is lost. It is known from this photograph by Alfred Stieglitz, published in the magazine The Blind Man in May 1917.
VAULT-544: Dalí painted this small canvas in 1931. The cliffs in the background are those of the Catalan coast near his home at Port Lligat. It was first shown at the Julien Levy Gallery in New York in 1932 and came to the Museum of Modern Art in 1934.
VAULT-553: Picasso painted this in Paris in May and June 1937 for the Spanish Republic's pavilion at the Paris International Exposition. It responds to the bombing of the Basque town of Guernica by German and Italian aircraft on 26 April 1937. It was kept at the Museum of Modern Art in New York for decades and went to Spain in 1981.
VAULT-554: Hopper finished this in January 1942, a few weeks after the attack on Pearl Harbor. He said it was suggested by a restaurant on Greenwich Avenue in New York where two streets meet. The Art Institute of Chicago bought it within months for 3,000 dollars.
LIT-599: Keats wrote this ode at Winchester in September 1819. It was published in 1820 in Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems, the last book he saw through the press. He died in Rome in February 1821, aged twenty-five.
LIT-660: These are the last lines of The Great Gatsby, published in New York in April 1925. The narrator, Nick Carraway, is on the beach behind Gatsby's empty house on Long Island. Fitzgerald wrote most of the book in France in 1924.
VAULT-866: Painted in September 1888 in Arles, in the south of France. It shows a café on the Place du Forum, and Van Gogh painted it outdoors at night. The canvas is unsigned, but he described it in his letters. It is in the Kröller-Müller Museum at Otterlo in the Netherlands.
VAULT-868: Photographed on 24 December 1968 by the astronaut William Anders from Apollo 8, the first crewed spacecraft to orbit the Moon. It shows the Earth above the lunar horizon. Anders took it on colour film with a hand-held Hasselblad camera through the spacecraft window.
VAULT-889: Carved in Rome in 1498 and 1499, when Michelangelo was in his early twenties, for the funeral chapel of the French cardinal Jean de Bilhères. It is the only work he signed. His name is cut into the band across Mary's chest. In 1972 a man attacked it with a hammer. It was restored and has stood behind glass in Saint Peter's Basilica since.
VAULT-905: Painted in 1599 and 1600 for the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi, the church of the French community in Rome. It was Caravaggio's first major public commission. It hangs in the chapel opposite his Martyrdom of Saint Matthew, painted at the same time. The scene is the moment in the Gospel when Christ calls the tax collector Matthew to follow him.
VAULT-906: Jean-Paul Marat, a journalist and leader of the French Revolution, was stabbed in his bath by Charlotte Corday on 13 July 1793. David was his friend and a fellow deputy, and he finished the picture within a few months. Marat worked in the bath because of a skin disease. David died in exile in Brussels in 1825, and the painting has been in the museum there since the late nineteenth century.
VAULT-908: One of the fourteen Black Paintings that Goya painted directly on the plaster walls of his house outside Madrid between about 1819 and 1823. He was in his seventies and deaf. He gave the pictures no titles and did not show them. In the 1870s, long after his death, they were cut from the walls and put on canvas, and in 1881 they were given to the Spanish state.
VAULT-910: The Temeraire was a 98-gun warship that fought at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805. In 1838 she was sold and towed up the Thames to Rotherhithe to be broken up. Turner showed the picture at the Royal Academy in 1839. He never sold it, and it came to the National Gallery with his bequest. It appears on the Bank of England twenty pound note issued in 2020.
VAULT-918: Painted in Delft around 1657 to 1660. The woman is a kitchen maid, not a milkmaid in the dairy sense, and she is pouring milk into an earthenware pot. The Rijksmuseum bought it in 1908 from the Six family collection in Amsterdam, with help from the Rembrandt Society and after a debate in the Dutch parliament.
VAULT-930: Painted in Amsterdam in 1633 and the only seascape Rembrandt is known to have painted. It shows the Gospel story of Christ calming the storm. Isabella Stewart Gardner bought it in 1898 for her museum in Boston. On 18 March 1990 thieves cut it from its frame and took it with twelve other works. None has been recovered.
VAULT-954: Van Gogh painted this in Antwerp in the winter of 1885 to 1886, while he was a student at the city's art academy. Drawing from skeletons was a standard part of academic training in anatomy. He left for Paris a few weeks later.
